title: Optimal-work feedback on particles with activity --- gliding on active fluctuations using positional information
authors: Lars Torbjørn Stutzer, Sarah A. M. Loos
abstract: We study the minimum-work feedback control of particles subject to active fluctuations. Considering an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle confined by a moving harmonic trap, we derive exact optimal protocols following an initial position measurement. Our results show that nonequilibrium correlations between position and active fluctuations allow work extraction from the activity based on positional information only, i.e., without directly measuring the active degree of freedom, which was the focus of earlier literature. We find that depending on the persistence time, activity can either facilitate or impede transport relative to passive systems. Surprisingly, unlike feedback schemes based on direct measurements of the active fluctuations, positional feedback remains energetically advantageous even in the limit of infinitely persistent activity. Our results provide design principles for information engines and optimal control strategies operating in active environments.
summary: This paper analyzes the minimum work required to control particles immersed in active fluctuating environments. It demonstrates that positional information alone can be used to extract energy from the activity, a finding that surpasses previous requirements for direct measurement of the active noise. The results offer crucial design principles for controlling systems in non-equilibrium active matter.
main_problem: The study focuses on determining the minimum work required for feedback control of particles subjected to active fluctuations, specifically investigating if work can be extracted using only positional measurements rather than direct measurements of the active degree of freedom.
main_result: Positional feedback alone is sufficient to efficiently harvest work from activity due to non-trivial correlations, and this positional feedback remains energetically advantageous even in the limit of infinitely persistent activity.
method: The authors use optimal control theory to derive optimal protocols and calculate the average minimum work input required to move a harmonic trap minimum, comparing results from positional vs. active-fluctuation measurements.
model_or_system: The model involves an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) confined by a moving harmonic trap. The dynamics are governed by overdamped Langevin equations incorporating active fluctuations that break detailed balance.
key_observables: Average minimum work input ($\langle W_\alpha[\lambda] angle$), optimal feedback protocols ($\lambda^*(s)$), and the comparison of work extracted using positional vs. active-fluctuation information.
important_parameters: Persistence time ($	au$), trap strength ($\kappa$), thermal diffusion ($\sigma$), and active fluctuation strength ($\sigma'$). The analysis examines limits like $	au 	o 0$ and $	au 	o \infty$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the joint stationary distribution is Gaussian. The comparison between different feedback schemes is central to the argument.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares the average optimal work ($	ext{Ex}_0[\dots]$) for positional feedback versus active-fluctuation feedback as a function of persistence time ($	au$), showing how the benefit of activity changes with $	au$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and control objective, derives the optimal protocols using variational methods, and then systematically compares the work extracted using positional information versus direct active fluctuation measurements, analyzing the asymptotic limits.
why_interesting: The work provides general design principles for information engines and optimal control strategies operating in non-equilibrium active environments, which is relevant to understanding energy transduction in complex biological or synthetic active matter systems.
